Issued at 105 AM MDT Sun Sep 6 2026

I was thinking back to where I was 18 years ago tonight. I had just 
finished my last shift at my previous job for a private company in 
Pennsylvania, and begin a 5000 mile drive to start my career in the 
National Weather Service, in Alaska. At this time I was sound asleep 
in a motel room in Sparta, Wisconsin. I was quite tired after 
driving 800 miles after working a midnight shift and having to 
endure the Chicago rush hour traffic. And this ties into the weather 
pattern coming up the next week, mainly with transitions and 
changes. As temperatures changed from the warm late summer 
temperatures in the lower 48 states then cooling as I drove 
northward, especially when I reached the Yukon, Northwest 
Territories and Alaska. This reminds me of the pattern over the next 
week, when we will see a little bit of everything. This includes 
some continued warm late summer temperatures, gusty to strong wind, 
elevated to potentially critical fire weather and maybe, just maybe, 
the first real taste of fall for next weekend.

Today will be another very warm day across the area as ridging holds 
for another day, with the warmest spots likely seeing highs around 
90. We have a couple of concerns over the next 24 hours. The first 
is, once again, fire weather. The set up looks similar to yesterday. 
Some areas will be see relative humidity under 15 percent, 
especially East of the Divide. Others will see a gusty afternoon 
wind, especially in southern Wyoming and West of the Divide. Most of 
these areas are not together though. With this, along with 
increasing cloud cover and dew points ticking higher later in the 
day, we will not issue any Red Flag Warnings. Elevated fire weather 
still looks likely though. The other concern, especially late today 
and especially tonight, will be the chance of showers and possible 
thunderstorms. Deeper moisture will moving into southwestern Wyoming 
later this afternoon, spreading across the area tonight. At this 
same time, an upper level low will be lifting northward in Idaho. 
This will drag a Pacific Cold Front and negatively tilted trough 
across the area. This will be a typical monsoon set up though, in 
that all areas will have a chance of showers, but not everyone will 
see one. Models have come into decent agreement in keeping the most 
numerous showers in western Wyoming, with lessening chances further 
east. We still have a marginal risk of excessive rainfall across 
this area as well. Precipitable water values will rise close to an 
inch in some locations, which is over 175 percent of normal. 
However, there is plenty of steering flow, with some 500 millibar 
winds approaching 50 knots. So, the main threat of from training 
storms. With the strong wind level wind as possible mixing from the 
frontal passage, there could be some strong wind gusts as well. The 
deepest moisture will be through the area by Monday morning, but a 
few showers will be possible into Monday with wrap-around moisture, 
mainly in the northern and western Wyoming.

Monday will be a cooler day behind the front. The main concern here 
shifts to wind. We will have a fairly pressure gradient between the 
low to the northwest and the ridge to the south and east. That means 
a gusty to potentially strong wind across much of the area. Much of 
the area, especially East of the Divide, has at least a 1 in 2 
chance of wind gusts past 35 mph. With 700 millibar winds 
approaching 40 knots at times, there could be some gusts to around 
50 mph, especially in the higher elevations and in some wind prone 
areas like the south side of Casper. As for fire weather, the wind 
will be there but there should be enough residual humidity to keep 
conditions above critical. It will be another day of elevated fire 
weather though. The real day of fire weather concern will be 
Tuesday, when dew points really crater and a gusty wind continues. 
As of now, there is at least a 2 out of 3 chance of seeing some Fire 
Weather Watches issued for this time period. Dry zonal flow will 
dominate through Friday with dry conditions, warm temperatures and a 
continued gusty breeze. Further fire weather highlights may be 
needed on these days bit wind may be borderline in some locations.

And now to the potential change I was talking about. The main word 
of this sentence is POTENTIAL, since this is a week out a lot can 
change between now and then. Both the European model and the 
GFS show a decent system coming out of Canada for the weekend. 
There are differences in timing and details, as would be 
expected this far out. In addition, the GFS has more of a front 
/ open wave while the European has a closed low. I won't even 
try to hash out the details at this point. However, the 
potential for the coolest temperatures we have seen since last 
spring are possible. Both models show below zero temperatures at
